lessons.title: Purpose and Methods of Degumming
lessons.body:
Crude oil straight from your press contains gumsâphosphatides, waxes, and other sticky substances. These gums cause problems: they make the oil cloudy, they burn and stick to your frying pan, and they shorten shelf life. Degumming removes them. In Africa, where many small producers sell to local markets and restaurants, degummed oil looks cleaner and lasts longer, which means better prices and less waste.

There are three main methods. Water degumming is the simplest: you add 2â3% hot water (about 70Â°C) to oil heated to 60â70Â°C, stir gently for 30â60 minutes, then let it settle. The gums absorb water, swell, and sink or can be centrifuged out. This works well for oils like sunflower and groundnut. Acid degumming uses food-grade phosphoric acid (0.05â0.2% of oil weight) or citric acid. The acid converts non-hydratable gums into hydratable ones, so they can be removed with water. This is better for oils like soy and palm that have more stubborn gums. Enzymatic degumming uses enzymes (phospholipases) at 50â60Â°C for 2â4 hours; itâs expensive and rarely used by small producers in Africa.

For a small-scale operation in Kenya, Nigeria, or Ghana, water degumming is the most practical. You need a stainless steel tank with a heating source, a stirrer, and a way to separate the gum layerâeither a settling tank with a bottom drain or a simple centrifuge. After degumming, the oil is heated to 90â100Â°C to evaporate residual water. Test for gums by heating a sample in a pan: if it browns and sticks, gums remain.

Degumming also protects downstream equipment. If you skip it, the neutralization step will use more chemicals and produce more soapstock. So always degum first. Store degummed oil in clean, dry containers to avoid rehydration of any leftover gums.

lessons.title: Water Degumming and Acid Degumming
lessons.body:
Water degumming is the go-to method for small and medium producers in Africa. Start with crude oil at 60â70Â°C. Add 2â3% clean water (by weight of oil) heated to about 70Â°C. Stir gently at 60â80 rpm for 30â60 minutes. Youâll see the oil turn cloudy as gums hydrate. Stop stirring and let the tank settle for 2â4 hours. The gums drop to the bottom as a thick, watery layer. Drain them off. Then heat the oil to 90â100Â°C for 30 minutes to drive off moisture. If you have a centrifuge, use it after stirring to speed separationâspin at 3000â4000 rpm.

For oils with high non-hydratable gums (like soy, palm, or cottonseed), water alone wonât work. Use acid degumming. First, heat oil to 60â70Â°C. Add food-grade phosphoric acid (0.05â0.2% of oil weight) or citric acid (0.1â0.3%) diluted in a little water. Mix for 15â20 minutes. Then add 2â3% hot water and stir for another 30â60 minutes. The acid breaks down metal-phosphatide complexes so the gums can absorb water. Let settle and drain. Finally, heat to 90â100Â°C to remove moisture.

In practice, many African processors combine methods: a small acid dose followed by water. This gives clearer oil and less gum residue. Always use stainless steel or enameled tanksâiron or copper will react with the acid and darken the oil. Test your degumming by heating a small sample in a frying pan. If it foams, spatters, or leaves a brown film, you need more acid or longer settling. Store degummed oil in clean, dry drums. Proper degumming reduces refining losses by 1â2% and improves the final oilâs color and stability.

lessons.title: Chemical Neutralization of Free Fatty Acids
lessons.body:
Free fatty acids (FFAs) are the enemy of good oil. They cause rancidity, off-flavors, and smoke at low temperatures. In Africa, where storage conditions can be hot and humid, FFAs rise quickly. Neutralization removes them by reacting with an alkaliâusually caustic soda (sodium hydroxide, NaOH). The reaction forms soap, which can be separated.

First, measure the FFA content. A simple titration kit is cheap and available from lab suppliers. For most edible oils, you want FFA below 0.1% after refining. If your crude oil has 2% FFA, you need about 0.14% NaOH (as a percentage of oil weight) for every 1% FFA, plus a small excess (0.05â0.1%) to drive the reaction. So for 100 kg oil with 2% FFA, use about 0.28â0.38 kg NaOH. Dissolve the NaOH in water to make a 10â20% solution. Heat the oil to 60â70Â°C. Add the caustic slowly with gentle stirring (60 rpm) for 15â20 minutes. Youâll see soapstock form as a curdy layer.

Stop stirring and let settle for 4â8 hours, or use a centrifuge. Drain the soapstock from the bottom. Then wash the oil with hot water (10â20% of oil volume) at 70â80Â°C to remove residual soap. Settle and drain again. Repeat washing if needed until the wash water is clear. Finally, dry the oil by heating to 90â100Â°C under vacuum or with gentle stirring until no bubbles form.

Safety: NaOH is corrosive. Wear gloves, goggles, and an apron. Always add NaOH to water, never water to NaOH. In Africa, many small refineries use this method successfully. It requires careful measurement and patience, but it turns poor-quality crude oil into clean, saleable cooking oil.

lessons.title: Soapstock Treatment and Utilization
lessons.body:
Soapstock is the thick, dark, soapy paste that settles out during neutralization. For every 100 kg of crude oil, you might get 5â15 kg of soapstock, depending on FFA content. Donât throw it awayâit has value. In Africa, soapstock can be a source of income or used on the farm.

The first step is to recover entrained oil. Soapstock contains 20â40% neutral oil. Heat the soapstock to 80â90Â°C with stirring, add 5â10% hot water, and let it settle. The oil floats and can be skimmed off. You can also add a little salt (1â2%) to help break the emulsion. This recovered oil can be added back to the next batch of crude oil or sold as technical oil for soap making.

After oil recovery, the remaining soapstock is rich in fatty acids and can be acidulated. Add sulfuric acid (10â20% solution) slowly until the pH drops to 2â3. This converts soaps back to free fatty acids, which float as a dark layer. This acid oil can be sold to soap factories, used as animal feed additive, or burned as fuel. In many African countries, thereâs a market for acid oil among local soap makers.

If you canât sell it, compost it. Soapstock is biodegradable, but itâs alkaline, so mix it with acidic materials like fruit waste or cow dung. It adds nutrients to the soil. Some farmers use it as a pest repellent when diluted with water. Never dump soapstock into rivers or streamsâit harms fish and plants. Store it in covered drums to prevent rain from washing it away. With a little effort, soapstock becomes a resource, not a waste.

lessons.title: Physical Refining vs. Chemical Refining
lessons.body:
After degumming, you have two main paths to remove free fatty acids: chemical refining (neutralization with caustic soda) or physical refining (steam distillation under vacuum). Each has pros and cons for African processors.

Chemical refining is what we covered in Lesson 3. It uses NaOH to neutralize FFAs, then washing and drying. It works well for oils with low to medium FFA (up to 5%) and is forgiving if you lack vacuum equipment. But it produces soapstock, uses water, and loses some neutral oil. Itâs the standard for small-scale operations in Africa because the equipment is simple: tanks, stirrers, and a heat source.

Physical refining uses high temperature (240â260Â°C) and vacuum (2â5 mbar) to steam-strip FFAs. It requires a vacuum pump, a deodorizer, and precise temperature control. Itâs more energy-intensive but produces less waste and higher yield. Itâs best for oils with high FFA (like palm oil, which can have 5â10% FFA) and for large-scale plants. In Africa, physical refining is used in big palm oil mills in Nigeria, Ghana, and CÃ´te dâIvoire, but itâs rare in small workshops because of the cost.

Which should you choose? If you process less than 1 ton per day, chemical refining is more practical. If you have access to reliable electricity and can afford the equipment, physical refining saves money on chemicals and reduces waste. Many medium-scale African processors use a hybrid: degum, then chemical neutralization for high-FFA oils, and physical refining for low-FFA oils like sunflower. Always calculate your FFA first. For FFA above 2%, physical refining may be cheaper in the long run. For FFA below 1%, chemical refining is fine. Consider your local market for soapstockâif you can sell it, chemical refining has an extra income stream.

lessons.title: Monitoring and Quality Control in Degumming and Neutralization
lessons.body:
Quality control (QC) is what separates a hobby from a business. In degumming and neutralization, you must test at every step. Without QC, you waste chemicals, lose oil, and produce inconsistent batches that customers wonât trust.

Start with the crude oil. Measure FFA by titration. A simple kit costs less than $50 and gives results in minutes. Also check moisture (using a moisture meter or by heating a sample and weighing) and impurities (filter a sample and weigh the residue). For degumming, test for gums by the âcold testâ: put a sample in an ice bath for 5 hours; if it clouds, gums remain. Or do a hot pan test: heat a tablespoon of oil in a pan; if it foams and spatters, degumming is incomplete.

During neutralization, monitor pH of the soapstock and the oil. After washing, the wash water should be neutral (pH 7). If itâs still soapy, wash again. After drying, check FFA againâit should be below 0.1% for good oil. Also measure color using a simple Lovibond comparator or a colorimeter. A good refined oil is light yellow to golden. If itâs dark, you may have used too much caustic or overheated.

Keep records: date, batch number, oil type, FFA before and after, chemicals used, temperatures, and yields. In Africa, where electricity can be unreliable, use manual thermometers and hydrometers. Train your workers to follow the same steps every time. A small notebook is your best QC tool. Finally, store samples from each batch for at least 3 months. If a customer complains, you can trace the problem. Good QC builds reputationâand in the cooking oil business, reputation is everything.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Oil Refining â Degumming and Neutralization

This practical reference is written for small and medium-sized African edible oil processors â from a 2 t/day batch plant in Uganda to a 50 t/day continuous refinery in Nigeria. It consolidates the six lessons of this module into shop-floor guidance: what to do, what to measure, what it costs, and where the money is made or lost. In crude vegetable oil, gums and free fatty acids (FFA) are not just quality problems â they are yield losses, energy costs, and the difference between selling at a discount or at a premium to a buyer, hotel, or supermarket chain.

1. Why Degumming and Neutralization Decide Your Margin

Crude oil from a screw press or expeller typically contains 0.5â3% phospholipids (gums) and 0.5â5% FFA depending on seed quality, storage, and pressing temperature. If you skip degumming, gums hydrate during storage and form a sludge that plugs filters, fouls the deodorizer, and causes the oil to darken and foam when heated â a fatal defect for frying oil sold to street-food vendors or restaurants. If you skip neutralization, high FFA oil smokes, tastes harsh, and oxidizes quickly, shortening shelf life and destroying repeat business.

Every 1% of FFA removed as soapstock is roughly 1% of your oil volume leaving as a by-product. Recovering and selling soapstock (or acid oil) is therefore a direct revenue stream, not just waste disposal. In Kenya, Nigeria, and Ghana, acid oil and soapstock are bought by soap makers, animal feed blenders, and oleochemical processors. Treating soapstock as a product rather than a cost is one of the fastest margin improvements available to an African refiner.

2. Degumming: Water vs. Acid â Choosing by Feedstock

Water degumming is the cheapest route and works well for oils where the phospholipids are hydratable â typical of good-quality groundnut, sunflower, and sesame oil. Add 2â3% hot water (70â80Â°C) to oil at 60â70Â°C, mix gently for 20â30 minutes, then separate by settling or centrifuge. The gums drop out and can be dried and sold as lecithin or feed ingredient.

Acid degumming (using food-grade phosphoric or citric acid) is needed when the oil contains non-hydratable phospholipids â common in cottonseed, soybean, and oils from damaged or poorly stored seed. Acid converts these gums into hydratable forms, allowing removal. For a small African processor, the practical decision rule is: if the oil comes from well-stored, freshly pressed seed and is destined for local frying oil, water degumming is usually sufficient. If the oil is for export, long shelf life, or comes from cottonseed/soybean, use acid degumming.

Table 1: Degumming method selection by feedstock and market
Feedstock / Situation Recommended Method Typical Water/Acid Dose Gum Removal Target Business Note
Fresh-pressed groundnut, sesame Water degumming 2â3% water, 70â80Â°C â¥90% phosphorus removed Lowest cost; gums can be sold as feed
Sunflower (good seed) Water degumming 2â3% water Phosphorus < 200 ppm Suitable for local frying oil
Cottonseed, soybean Acid degumming 0.05â0.2% phosphoric/citric acid Phosphorus < 30 ppm Required for export / long shelf life
Poorly stored or damaged seed Acid degumming + extra wash Acid then 5â10% water wash Phosphorus < 50 ppm Higher chemical cost, but avoids rejection

Sources: FAO Agricultural Services Bulletin 94 (Small-scale oil extraction from groundnuts and copra); Practical Action, Small-Scale Vegetable Oil Processing; and industry degumming practice compiled by the American Oil Chemists' Society (AOCS) refining guidelines.

3. Chemical Neutralization: The Core Yield Decision

Neutralization uses caustic soda (NaOH) or caustic potash (KOH) to convert FFA into soap, which is then separated. The amount of caustic needed depends on FFA content, the oil type, and the desired excess. A common rule of thumb for batch refining is:

NaOH required (kg per tonne oil) â [0.142 Ã FFA%] + excess (0.05â0.15%)

For example, an oil with 3% FFA needs roughly 0.43 kg NaOH per 100 kg oil plus a small excess. Over-dosing wastes caustic and increases neutral oil loss through saponification; under-dosing leaves FFA behind. The soapstock yield is roughly proportional to FFA removed, but typically includes 20â50% neutral oil entrained â this is where money is lost. Good temperature control (60â80Â°C), gentle agitation, and prompt separation minimize entrainment.

Table 2: Typical neutralization operating parameters and expected outcomes
Parameter Batch Refining Continuous Refining Why It Matters
Oil temperature 60â70Â°C 75â90Â°C Too low = poor reaction; too high = dark color
Caustic concentration 10â16 Â°BÃ© 12â20 Â°BÃ© Controls soap density and separation speed
Excess caustic 0.05â0.15% 0.05â0.10% Excess reduces FFA but raises oil loss
Mixing time 15â30 min Seconds (in-line) Long mixing increases neutral oil entrainment
Expected FFA after neutralization <0.1% <0.05% Specification for edible/refined oil
Neutral oil loss 1.5â3.0 Ã FFA% 1.0â1.5 Ã FFA% Direct yield loss; minimize by good separation

Sources: FAO Agricultural Services Bulletin 94; AOCS refining practice notes; Practical Action oil processing guides. Values are typical ranges â always confirm with a laboratory titration on your own feedstock.

â  SAFETY WARNING â CAUSTIC SODA (NaOH) AND HOT OIL

Caustic soda causes severe chemical burns to eyes and skin, and can blind. Hot oil at 60â90Â°C causes serious scalds. Always wear chemical splash goggles, face shield, rubber gloves, apron, and closed boots when handling caustic or hot oil. Never add water to caustic â always add caustic slowly to water, stirring, in a well-ventilated area. Keep a clean water source and eyewash within 10 seconds of the workstation. Store caustic in clearly labeled, locked containers away from acids, and train every operator on first aid. In many African jurisdictions, caustic soda is a controlled industrial chemical â keep purchase and usage records for inspectors and buyers.

4. Soapstock: Turn a Waste Cost into a Revenue Line

Soapstock from neutralization typically contains 30â60% water, 20â50% soap, and 5â20% entrained neutral oil. Options for African processors:

  • Sell wet soapstock to local soap makers â simplest, lowest capital, but low price and heavy transport cost.
  • Acidulate to acid oil using sulfuric acid â recovers fatty acids and some neutral oil; acid oil sells to soap, feed, and oleochemical buyers at a higher price than wet soapstock.
  • Recover entrained neutral oil by heating and settling or centrifuging â directly increases edible oil yield.
  • Use as animal feed ingredient only after proper treatment and with veterinary/feed-safety approval; raw soapstock is high in salt and moisture.

Effluent from washing and acidulation must be treated â high pH, oil, and COD will fail environmental inspections and can contaminate local water. Simple settling ponds, pH neutralization, and oil traps are minimum requirements in most African regulatory contexts.

5. Physical vs. Chemical Refining â Which Fits Your Business?

Physical refining (steam stripping under vacuum) removes FFA without caustic, producing less soapstock and higher yield, but requires reliable vacuum, high-temperature steam, and consistent degumming to very low phosphorus (<10 ppm). It suits larger, well-capitalized plants processing palm, coconut, or well-degummed sunflower. Chemical refining is more forgiving, works at smaller scale, and is the default for most African SMEs â especially where feedstock quality varies and capital is limited. The business rule: choose physical refining only if you can consistently degum to <10 ppm phosphorus and maintain vacuum/steam systems; otherwise chemical refining will give more stable quality and fewer rejected batches.

6. Monitoring and Quality Control

You cannot manage what you do not measure. Minimum QC for a small refinery:

  • FFA titration on every incoming crude batch and every neutralized batch.
  • Phosphorus or simple gum test (hot water test) after degumming.
  • Soap content in washed oil (hot water + phenolphthalein).
  • Moisture and volatile matter after drying.
  • Color (Lovibond) and peroxide value for finished oil.
  • Record caustic used, oil in, oil out, soapstock out â this is your yield and margin dashboard.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Test FFA and gum content of every crude oil batch before deciding degumming method.
  2. Use water degumming for good-quality groundnut/sunflower/sesame; acid degumming for cottonseed, soybean, or damaged seed.
  3. Calculate caustic dose from FFA% (0.142 Ã FFA% + 0.05â0.15% excess) â never guess.
  4. Hold neutralization at 60â80Â°C with gentle mixing; separate soapstock promptly to reduce oil loss.
  5. Wash neutralized oil until soap content is negligible; dry before bleaching/deodorizing.
  6. Recover or sell soapstock/acid oil â treat it as a product, not waste.
  7. Wear full PPE for caustic and hot oil; keep eyewash and clean water at the workstation.
  8. Record oil in, oil out, chemical used, and by-product sold for every batch â review weekly against yield targets.

Further Reading

  • FAO Agricultural Services Bulletin 94 â Small-scale oil extraction from groundnuts and copra
  • Practical Action â Small-Scale Vegetable Oil Processing (technical briefs and publications)
  • FAO â Small-scale palm oil processing in Africa (Agricultural Services Bulletin 148)
  • American Oil Chemists' Society (AOCS) â Official Methods and Recommended Practices (FFA, phosphorus, soap)
  • WHO/FAO â Codex Alimentarius standards for edible fats and oils

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of degumming crude oil?
options: A) To remove free fatty acids
B) To remove phosphatides and other gums
quiz.explanation: Degumming specifically targets gums like phosphatides, which cause cloudiness and sticking.

quiz.q: Which method is most practical for small-scale African producers to remove gums?
quiz.explanation: Water degumming uses simple equipment and is effective for many oils like sunflower and groundnut.

quiz.q: What percentage of hot water is typically added during water degumming?
quiz.explanation: 2â3% water by weight of oil is standard to hydrate gums without excessive dilution.

quiz.q: Which acid is commonly used in acid degumming?
quiz.explanation: Food-grade phosphoric acid (or citric acid) is used to convert non-hydratable gums.

quiz.q: What temperature should oil be heated to during water degumming?
quiz.explanation: 60â70Â°C is optimal for gum hydration and separation.

quiz.q: After degumming, why is the oil heated to 90â100Â°C?
quiz.explanation: Heating drives off moisture that could cause hydrolysis and rancidity.

quiz.q: What is a simple test to check if degumming is complete?
options: B) Heat a sample in a pan and look for foaming
quiz.explanation: If gums remain, the oil will foam and spatter when heated.

quiz.q: Which oil type typically requires acid degumming instead of water degumming?
quiz.explanation: Soybean oil has non-hydratable gums that need acid to be removed.

quiz.q: What is the primary chemical used in neutralization of free fatty acids?
quiz.explanation: Sodium hydroxide (caustic soda) reacts with FFAs to form soap.

quiz.q: For 100 kg of oil with 2% FFA, approximately how much NaOH is needed?
quiz.explanation: 0.14% NaOH per 1% FFA plus excess gives about 0.28â0.38 kg for 2% FFA.

quiz.q: What is the target FFA level after neutralization for good edible oil?
quiz.explanation: High-quality refined oil should have FFA below 0.1% to prevent rancidity.

quiz.q: Why should you never add water to NaOH?
options: A) It causes a violent exothermic reaction
B) It dilutes the NaOH too much
quiz.explanation: Adding water to NaOH can cause a dangerous splash and heat spike; always add NaOH to water.

quiz.q: What is soapstock?
options: C) A type of bleaching earth
quiz.explanation: Soapstock is the soapy layer formed when NaOH reacts with FFAs.

quiz.q: How can you recover oil from soapstock?
options: B) Add water and salt, then heat and settle
quiz.explanation: Heating with water and salt helps break the emulsion and release entrained oil.

quiz.q: What is acid oil?
options: A) Oil treated with acid during degumming
B) Oil recovered from soapstock after acidulation
quiz.explanation: Acidulation of soapstock converts soaps back to free fatty acids, forming acid oil.

quiz.q: Which is a safe way to dispose of soapstock if you cannot sell it?
quiz.explanation: Composting with acidic materials neutralizes alkalinity and adds nutrients to soil.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between chemical and physical refining?
options: A) Chemical uses steam, physical uses caustic
B) Chemical uses caustic, physical uses steam distillation
C) Chemical is for large scale, physical for small scale
D) Chemical removes gums, physical removes FFAs
quiz.explanation: Chemical refining neutralizes FFAs with caustic; physical refining strips FFAs with steam under vacuum.

quiz.q: Which refining method is more suitable for high-FFA oils like crude palm oil?
quiz.explanation: Physical refining is more efficient for high-FFA oils and produces less waste.

quiz.q: What equipment is essential for physical refining but not for chemical refining?
quiz.explanation: Physical refining requires vacuum to lower the boiling point of FFAs.

quiz.q: For a small-scale African processor with less than 1 ton/day, which refining method is more practical?
quiz.explanation: Chemical refining uses simpler equipment and is more forgiving for small operations.

quiz.q: What is the first step in quality control for degumming and neutralization?
options: A) Measure FFA of crude oil
quiz.explanation: Knowing the initial FFA determines how much caustic to use.

quiz.q: How can you test for residual gums after degumming?
quiz.explanation: The cold test (ice bath for 5 hours) shows cloudiness if gums remain.

quiz.q: After neutralization and washing, what should the pH of the wash water be?
quiz.explanation: Neutral wash water indicates all soap has been removed.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep records in oil refining?
options: B) To trace problems and ensure consistency
quiz.explanation: Records help identify issues and replicate good batches.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool for measuring color of refined oil?
quiz.explanation: Lovibond comparators are affordable and give a standard color reading.

quiz.q: What should you do if refined oil is darker than expected?
options: B) Check for overheating or excess caustic
quiz.explanation: Dark color often results from high temperatures or too much NaOH.

quiz.q: How long should you store samples from each batch?
quiz.explanation: 3 months allows for customer complaint investigation and quality tracking.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake in neutralization that leads to high refining losses?
quiz.explanation: Excess caustic saponifies neutral oil, increasing losses.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a method of degumming?
quiz.explanation: Steam stripping is part of physical refining, not degumming.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature for drying oil after washing?
quiz.explanation: 90â100Â°C evaporates water without damaging the oil.
